account: Julapa Jagtiani of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and Catharine Lemieux of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago wrote Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia working paper 18–15, revised January 2019. Its title is “The Roles of Alternative Data and Machine Learning in Fintech Lending: Evidence from the LendingClub Consumer Platform”. It compares account-level LendingClub loans with similar loans in Y-14M reports from bank holding companies with assets of $50 billion or more. The authors report that the correlation between LendingClub's rating grades and FICO scores declined. It was about 80 percent for 2007 originations and about 35 percent for 2014–2015 vintages. They report that the grades perform well in predicting loan performance over the two years after origination. Alternative data allowed some borrowers who would have been classified as subprime by traditional criteria to be slotted into better grades. They got lower-priced credit. For the same default risk consumers pay smaller spreads at LendingClub than on credit cards. For 2015 loans about 8 percent of A-rated and 28 percent of B-rated borrowers had FICO scores below 680. The working paper itself gives only a month for its revision. The study passed peer review and appeared in Financial Management on 6 November 2019 (DOI 10.1111/fima.12295). In a working paper dated 26 October 2023, Jagtiani, Lemieux and Brandon Goldstein reported that LendingClub's grades kept predicting default through the COVID-19 pandemic. They add that the grades predicted default less well during the pandemic than before it. They also found that nonprime LendingClub borrowers defaulted much less often than nonprime credit card borrowers. They report that LendingClub kept lending to nonprime borrowers during its tightening of 2019.

ai_role.statement: The paper attributes the regrading of subprime borrowers to alternative data used by the lender. It does not establish that machine learning produced the grades. LendingClub developed and deployed its own model. The Federal Reserve authors are independent.

fields.account: Julapa Jagtiani of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia and Catharine Lemieux of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago wrote Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia working paper 18–15, revised January 2019. Its title is “The Roles of Alternative Data and Machine Learning in Fintech Lending: Evidence from the LendingClub Consumer Platform”. It compares account-level LendingClub loans with similar loans in Y-14M reports from bank holding companies with assets of $50 billion or more. The authors report that the correlation between LendingClub's rating grades and FICO scores declined. It was about 80 percent for 2007 originations and about 35 percent for 2014–2015 vintages. They report that the grades perform well in predicting loan performance over the two years after origination. Alternative data allowed some borrowers who would have been classified as subprime by traditional criteria to be slotted into better grades. They got lower-priced credit. For the same default risk consumers pay smaller spreads at LendingClub than on credit cards. For 2015 loans about 8 percent of A-rated and 28 percent of B-rated borrowers had FICO scores below 680. The working paper itself gives only a month for its revision. The study passed peer review and appeared in Financial Management on 6 November 2019 (DOI 10.1111/fima.12295). In a working paper dated 26 October 2023, Jagtiani, Lemieux and Brandon Goldstein reported that LendingClub's grades kept predicting default through the COVID-19 pandemic. They add that the grades predicted default less well during the pandemic than before it. They also found that nonprime LendingClub borrowers defaulted much less often than nonprime credit card borrowers. They report that LendingClub kept lending to nonprime borrowers during its tightening of 2019.

ratings.reason: Borrowers with subprime FICO scores who received better grades paid less for credit, and LendingClub borrowers paid smaller spreads than credit card borrowers with the same default risk. The sources report a cost saving, measured across loan vintages.
Financial-inclusion effects are discussed at the aggregate level only.
